unit.title: Racecraft: how passing really works
unit.summary: Why followers are slower, how drivers gain on straights, braking duels, defending, and the start.

lessons.title: Dirty air
lessons.objective: Explain why a following car loses grip and overheats its tyres.

payload.prompt: Why is the air behind a leading car called dirty air?

options.text: It is turbulent from the car ahead and breaks down the follower's downforce.
options.explanation: Right. The wake is fast-moving, chaotic air that the follower's wings cannot use.

options.text: The leading car's exhaust dirties the air for followers.
options.explanation: Not the main reason. It is the aerodynamic wake from the car body and wings.

options.text: Dirt from the track blows up behind the car.
options.explanation: No. Dirty air is an F1 aerodynamic term, not literal dust.

options.text: The leader's brake dust clouds the view.
options.explanation: That is not why it is called dirty air in F1.

explanation.correct: Right. Dirty air is the turbulent wake behind a car. The faster air breaks up the downforce the follower needs to turn.
explanation.incorrect: Dirty air is the aerodynamic wake behind a car. Turbulence from the body and wings makes the follower lose grip and overheat tyres.
explanation.sayThisLine: That wake is dirty air, and it ruins the downforce for anyone behind.

payload.prompt: Why do a follower's tyres degrade faster in dirty air?

options.text: Less grip from the broken downforce means the driver slides more and stresses the tyres.
options.explanation: Right. No downforce, more sliding, tyres overheat and die faster.

options.text: Debris from the car ahead damages the follower's tyres.
options.explanation: Not the main reason. It is the loss of downforce and tyre overheating.

options.text: Dirty air is hotter and burns the rubber faster.
options.explanation: The issue is that the follower slides more, overheating the tyres from inside.

options.text: Followers always drive more aggressively in dirty air.
options.explanation: Some do, but the tyre damage is mainly from loss of downforce and sliding.

explanation.correct: Right. Less downforce means more sliding, which overheats and stresses the tyres. A follower burns out tyres much faster than the leader.
explanation.incorrect: Dirty air breaks downforce. Without grip, the follower slides more, and sliding generates heat. Overheated tyres degrade quickly.
explanation.sayThisLine: No downforce, more sliding, tyres die faster.

payload.prompt: Your tyres are cooking in his dirty air and no pass is on. Back off a little, or stay close?

scene.alt: Text only: a following car sitting half a second behind a rival, its tyre temperatures climbing.

explanation.correct: Right. Following closely costs grip and overheats the tyres. Dropping back a little gives cleaner air and cooler tyres, which can save the stint while you wait for a real chance.
explanation.incorrect: Staying right behind means constant dirty air, more sliding and hotter tyres. If there is no pass on, giving yourself a gap can help the tyres last and keep the option open for later.
explanation.sayThisLine: He backed off a bit to save his tyres from the dirty air.

payload.prompt: Is dirty air worse for the follower in fast corners or slow corners?

scene.alt: Two corner scenarios: slow hairpin and high-speed turn.

explanation.correct: Right. Downforce does more of the work the faster you go, so losing it in a fast corner costs the most. Slow corners depend more on mechanical grip.
explanation.incorrect: Dirty air hurts most where downforce matters most. High-speed corners need a lot of aerodynamic grip, so the follower loses the most there.
explanation.sayThisLine: Dirty air really hurts in the fast corners.

payload.prompt: The leader's tyres are fine but the follower's are overheating. Track heat or dirty air?

scene.alt: Temperature gauge showing high tyre temps for following car.

explanation.correct: Right. Both cars are on the same track, so the track cannot explain the difference. The follower slides more in dirty air and heats its tyres that way.
explanation.incorrect: The follower is sliding more because of less downforce in dirty air. That internal heat from sliding is what kills the tyres.
explanation.sayThisLine: Sliding overheats tyres. Dirty air causes sliding.

lessons.title: The tow
lessons.objective: Use the slipstream to gain speed and time the move.

payload.prompt: Where do drivers get a tow on a lap?

options.text: The straights, where the car ahead pushes the air aside and cuts the follower's drag.
options.explanation: Right. The tow is a drag advantage on straights. In corners, the follower sees dirty air.

options.text: Every part of the lap, including corners.
options.explanation: No. In corners, dirty air ruins downforce. Tow is a straight-line drag advantage only.

options.text: Only at the start, when cars are bunched.
options.explanation: No. Drivers use the tow throughout the race on every straight.

options.text: Nowhere; the tow is a myth.
options.explanation: The tow is real. It is a speed gain from reduced drag on straights.

explanation.correct: Right. On a straight, the car ahead punches a hole in the air. The follower sits in that wake, feels less drag and gains top speed.
explanation.incorrect: The tow is a straight-line effect: less air resistance for the car in the wake. In corners, the same wake is dirty air that costs grip.
explanation.sayThisLine: The tow is a drag advantage on straights.

payload.prompt: How close must the follower be to benefit from the tow?

options.text: Close behind, within about a second, and the closer the bigger the effect.
options.explanation: Right. The wake is strongest right behind the car ahead and fades as the gap grows.

options.text: Only when touching the car ahead's gearbox.
options.explanation: No contact is needed. A car a little further back still gets a useful tow.

options.text: Distance does not matter; the tow works from anywhere behind.
options.explanation: No. The tow fades quickly with distance. Several seconds back, there is essentially no tow.

options.text: Only when three or more seconds behind.
options.explanation: That is far too far back. The wake has mostly disappeared by then.

explanation.correct: Right. The tow works best when the follower is close, within about a second, and it grows the closer you get. Further back, the air has mixed and the benefit is gone.
explanation.incorrect: The tow is strongest right behind the car ahead and fades with distance. Being close, within about a second, is what gives a useful drag reduction.
explanation.sayThisLine: He is in the tow, so the car ahead is going to struggle.

payload.prompt: Best time to use the tow: on a long straight or a short one?

scene.alt: Two track layouts: one with a long back straight, one with a short straight.

explanation.correct: Right. A long straight gives more time to use the tow, build speed, and line up the braking-zone move.
explanation.incorrect: A long straight lets you follow, build speed from the tow, and make a cleaner pass. Short straights do not give enough room.
explanation.sayThisLine: Long straights, big tows, big passes.

lessons.title: The braking-zone duel
lessons.objective: Choose a sensible place and line to attack a braking zone.

payload.prompt: You have a great run on the car ahead into a tight right-hander. What is your move?

situation.narrative: You have pulled out of his tow at the end of a long straight and are right behind him. The braking zone for a tight right-hander is coming up.

facts.label: Corner
facts.value: Tight right-hander after a long straight

options.label: Brake a touch later on the inside and get alongside first
options.consequence: You use the speed from the tow to get level on the inside before he turns in. Being alongside means he has to leave you room, and you can make the pass stick if you carry enough exit speed.
considerations: The tow gives you the speed to get alongside before the braking zone.
Being properly alongside at the apex gives you a right to room.
Brake late enough to get level, not so late that you lock up.

options.label: Stay back, then dive in from well behind at the last moment
options.consequence: A lunge from too far back usually ends with a lock-up, a missed apex or contact. You may also be blamed by the stewards for causing the collision.
considerations: If you are not alongside at the apex, the other driver owes you nothing.
Locking up also flat-spots the tyre for the rest of the stint.

options.label: Stay behind and wait for a better corner
options.consequence: You keep your tyres and your race safe, but you waste a good run and may not get another chance this lap.
considerations: Patience is fine when a pass is not on.
Here you have speed, fresher tyres and the inside line, so the chance is a real one.

payload.expertNote: A pass is won by getting alongside before the corner, not by lunging from behind. Use the tow to pull level on the brakes, then let the rules give you the room you have earned.
payload.sayThisLine: He used the tow, got alongside on the brakes and made it stick.

payload.prompt: A rival squeezes you toward the edge in a fast corner. What do you do?

situation.narrative: You are alongside on the outside of a fast, sweeping left-hander, with your rival on the inside. At the apex he drifts wide and pushes you toward the edge of the track.

options.label: Hold your line and accept the contact
options.consequence: You both crash or one of you goes off. Contact at speed in a fast corner is dangerous and likely a DNF.
considerations: High-speed contact is a crash, not a racing incident.
Even if the stewards penalise him later, you would still be out of the race.
It is not worth a DNF.

options.label: Lift off and tuck in behind, try again next corner
options.consequence: You avoid a crash, stay in the race, and live to attack again on a safer corner.
considerations: You may lose the place, but you stay close and the stewards can look at his move.
The next corner or straight gives you a cleaner opportunity.
Staying in the race beats a DNF every time.

options.label: Run wide, stay ahead, risk the run-off area
options.consequence: You might stay on the track, or you might lock a tyre and slide off. It is a big gamble at this speed.
considerations: The edge of the track is close, and leaving it can also cost you a penalty.
If a tyre locks at this speed, your race is over.

payload.expertNote: At high speed, holding your line against a squeeze means contact. Lifting keeps you in the race, and the stewards can judge whether he left you room. You can try again on a safer corner or straight.
payload.sayThisLine: He lifted, stayed safe and went again on the next straight.

payload.prompt: Is a shallow dive into a 180-degree hairpin riskier or safer than a deep dive?

scene.alt: Racing scenario into a tight hairpin corner.

explanation.correct: Right. A hairpin is slow and tight. Deep = late braking and lock-up risk. Shallow lets you blend in and keep pace.
explanation.incorrect: A 180-degree hairpin is tight and slow. Late braking (deep dive) riskslock-up and running wide. A controlled, shallow entry is safer.
explanation.sayThisLine: Late braking kills at tight corners.

payload.prompt: Best corner for a pass: tight hairpin or long sweeper?

scene.alt: Two corners: a slow hairpin and a fast, long-radius turn.

explanation.correct: Right. Hairpins are slow, low-speed, long braking zones. Easy to follow, room to pass inside or out.
explanation.incorrect: Hairpins have long braking zones and low speed. Passes are clean there. Long sweepers are high-speed and hard to follow; braking zones are shorter.
explanation.sayThisLine: Hairpins are overtaking zones.

lessons.title: Defending without a penalty
lessons.objective: Apply the rules about moving under braking and leaving room.

payload.prompt: A car is alongside into a braking zone. Can you move right, then left to block?

situation.narrative: On a straight into a left-hander, a rival is alongside. You brake. He is on the right. You move right to cover him, then move left again to block the inside line.

options.label: Yes, you are entitled to defend the line as your right.
options.consequence: The stewards will penalise you. You made two moves under braking, and the rules allow one.
considerations: Defending the inside is fine. Moving twice is not.
Once you move right to cover, that is your move. You cannot move left again while braking.
The penalty is usually 5 seconds or a grid drop.

options.label: No; you can make one move, not two. Choose left to block or right to cover.
options.consequence: You defend legally. Pick one direction and commit. If he gets alongside, that is racing.
considerations: One move under braking; that is the rule.
Pick the line that suits your car and the corner.
If he is alongside after one move, he earned it, and you can still race him into the corner.

options.label: No defending at all; let him by and re-pass later.
options.consequence: You stay legal and avoid a penalty, but you lose the position and must out-race him elsewhere.
considerations: Playing it safe works sometimes, but you lose track position.
If he is not actually ahead, you should defend once.
Caving in every time is not racecraft.

payload.expertNote: One move under braking; that is the rule. Block the inside, or cover the outside, but not both. Pick your defence and hold it.

payload.prompt: A rival is on the inside line. Can you close the door gradually as you both turn in?

situation.narrative: Into a left-hander, a rival took the inside line. You are on the outside. As you both turn in, you gradually move left to close the gap between you and the kerb.

facts.label: Rival's car
facts.value: Still on the line, not pushed off

options.label: Yes, gradual closing is legal defence; he chose the inside risk.
options.consequence: You defend the corner legally. He knew the risk of the inside line; if he makes it stick, he earned it.
considerations: Closing down gradually in the turn-in is not a sudden move under braking.
The inside is riskier; if he cannot stay on the road, that is on him.
Stewards usually allow this as long as you do not force him off.

options.label: No, you must give him room or it is a penalty.
options.consequence: You are being cautious. You leave room and he gets the corner, but you stay legal and live to fight later.
considerations: Leaving room is the safest option.
But gradual closure in a turn-in is often allowed.
If you are unsure, the safe play is to give room.

options.label: No, a hard squeeze forces him off and will be penalised.
options.consequence: If you shut the door suddenly, you are right. Stewards penalise dangerous defending.
considerations: There is a difference between gradual and sudden.
A hard slam into the corner after he commits is dangerous.
Gradually closing as you both turn in is different from suddenly slamming the door.

payload.expertNote: Gradual closure in the turn-in is legal defence. Sudden, hard squeezing that forces a rival off is not. The difference is what stewards look for.
payload.sayThisLine: Gradual squeeze is racing; hard slam is a penalty.

payload.prompt: Can you move side to side under braking to block multiple passing lines?

scene.alt: Defending car moving left and right under braking.

choices.label: Yes, all defensive moves are legal
No, only one move under braking

explanation.correct: Right. Under braking, you get one move to block a line. Weaving is a penalty.
explanation.incorrect: One move under braking; that is the rule. Multiple moves to block are dangerous and penalised.

payload.prompt: You squeeze a rival so close he loses grip and almost crashes. Is that legal?

scene.alt: Two cars side-by-side, one squeezed to the edge of the track.

choices.label: Yes, he chose the inside risk

explanation.correct: Right. Unsafe, aggressive defending is penalised. You must leave racing room even in defence.
explanation.incorrect: Defence has limits. Forcing a car to lose control or run off is dangerous and merits a penalty.

payload.prompt: Where does the rule say you must leave room: braking zone or corner entry?

scene.alt: Racing scenario showing braking zone and corner entry.

explanation.correct: Right. At turn-in, you must leave a car width of room for a car that is alongside.
explanation.incorrect: The rule is at corner entry (turn-in). You must leave room if a car is alongside when you both commit to the corner.

payload.prompt: Best way to defend against a late-braking dive to the inside?

options.text: Block the inside line from the start and do not move.
options.explanation: Good, but you must allow it if he is truly alongside at turn-in.

options.text: Take a normal driving line and leave a car width at turn-in if needed.
options.explanation: Right. Defend by precision and line choice, but follow the room rule.

options.text: Squeeze him off the road; he chose the gamble.
options.explanation: No. Even on a dive-bomb, you must leave racing room at turn-in.

options.text: Brake early to get off the line and let him miss the apex.
options.explanation: Risky. You sacrifice braking distance and might run wide yourself.

explanation.correct: Right. Defend with precision: a perfect line and a quick apex. If he is alongside at turn-in, leave him room. That is racing.
explanation.incorrect: Defence is about line choice and precision, not brute force. Leave a car width at turn-in if he earns it with a real move.
explanation.sayThisLine: Defence is racing, not blocking.

lessons.title: Passing without DRS
lessons.objective: Explain how tow, Overtake Mode and wake combine to enable a pass.

payload.prompt: What does Overtake Mode do in 2026?

options.text: A boost button that lets the driver add extra electrical power when within one second of the car ahead.
options.explanation: Right. It replaces DRS and is available to the car being passed, not the leader.

options.text: The same as DRS: open the rear wing for a speed boost.
options.explanation: No. Overtake Mode is electrical. DRS is gone. Open the wings and you lose downforce in the corner.

options.text: A penalty given to the leader for defending too much.
options.explanation: No. Overtake Mode is a boost for the follower.

options.text: A rule that says you cannot defend more than once.
options.explanation: That is a defending rule, not Overtake Mode.

explanation.correct: Right. Overtake Mode is 2026's answer to DRS. An electrical boost for a car within one second of the leader, no wing needed.
explanation.incorrect: Overtake Mode is an electrical system in 2026. A car within one second of the car ahead gets a boost button. No DRS, no wing flaps.
explanation.sayThisLine: Overtake Mode replaced DRS.

payload.prompt: How do tow and Overtake Mode work together for a pass?

options.text: The follower gets a tow on the straight, builds speed, and the boost kicks in just before braking.
options.explanation: Right. The tow closes the gap; the boost gives an extra edge for the move.

options.text: Overtake Mode cancels the tow effect.
options.explanation: No. They work together. Close tow, then boost.

options.text: Only Overtake Mode matters; the tow is useless in 2026.
options.explanation: No. The tow is still important. Close follow, tow gain, boost gain, pass.

options.text: The leader can also use Overtake Mode to pull away.
options.explanation: No. Only the car within one second of the leader gets the boost.

explanation.correct: Right. The follower uses the tow to get close and build speed, then the Overtake Mode boost is the final kick into the braking zone.
explanation.incorrect: Tow + boost is the 2026 overtaking formula. Close follow for the tow, then add the electrical push to make the pass stick.
explanation.sayThisLine: Tow closes the gap; boost closes the deal.

payload.prompt: Why is dirty air a problem even with Overtake Mode?

options.text: The boost does not help in corners; dirty air costs grip, and the follower cannot corner as fast.
options.explanation: Right. Electrical boost only helps on straights. In corners, dirty air is still deadly.

options.text: Dirty air cancels Overtake Mode entirely.
options.explanation: No. The boost still works; it just does not fix the corner problem.

options.text: Overtake Mode solves the dirty air problem completely.
options.explanation: No. The boost is straight-line only. Dirty air ruins corners.

options.text: Dirty air only affects the leader, not the follower.
options.explanation: Wrong. Dirty air affects the follower's grip in corners.

explanation.correct: Right. Overtake Mode is a straight-line tool. In corners, the follower is still in dirty air and loses downforce and grip.
explanation.incorrect: Overtake Mode helps on straights. But corners are still dirty-air territory for the follower, which is why passes are often on big straights.
explanation.sayThisLine: Boost works on straights; dirty air kills in corners.

lessons.title: Lapped cars and blue flags
lessons.objective: Explain how traffic affects the leader and what the flags demand.

payload.prompt: What does a blue flag tell a lapped car to do?

options.text: Let the faster car through; you are being lapped and must yield.
options.explanation: Right. Blue flag means get out of the way. Ignore it and you get penalised.

options.text: Pit immediately; your car is damaged.
options.explanation: No. That is not what blue means. Blue is a lapping signal only.

options.text: Slow down a bit; the car behind is close.
options.explanation: No. Blue means you are lapped and must let him pass.

options.text: Keep the inside line; a lapped car is behind you.
options.explanation: Wrong. Blue tells the lapped car to yield.

explanation.correct: Right. A blue flag tells a lapped car to yield the racing line and let the faster car through. Ignoring it is a penalty.
explanation.incorrect: Blue flag is the lapping signal. If you are lapped and shown blue, you must yield safely as soon as possible.
explanation.sayThisLine: Blue flag means get out of the way.

payload.prompt: How does lapped traffic affect the race leader?

options.text: Lapped cars disrupt the leader's rhythm and gap management; must navigate them safely.
options.explanation: Right. Even at a huge pace advantage, lapped cars are traffic, and hitting one is a DNF.

options.text: Lapped cars help the leader by making passes for second place harder.
options.explanation: True sometimes, but lapped traffic is mainly a hazard for everyone.

options.text: Lapped traffic does not affect the leader; only second place feels it.
options.explanation: Wrong. The leader must navigate them and avoid crashes.

options.text: The FIA removes all lapped cars so the leader can race alone.
options.explanation: No. Lapped cars stay on track and are part of the race.

explanation.correct: Right. Even a dominant leader must navigate lapped cars. Crashing into one is a DNF, no matter how fast you are.
explanation.incorrect: Lapped traffic is a hazard for everyone. The leader must pass them safely, and a mistake costs the race.
explanation.sayThisLine: Lapped cars are part of the race for everyone.

payload.prompt: Is ignoring a blue flag a time penalty or a black flag?

scene.alt: Lapped car ignoring blue flag signal.

explanation.correct: Right. Repeated blue-flag ignoring gets a time penalty. A black flag is for much worse offences.
explanation.incorrect: Ignoring blue flags is dangerous driving and merits a time penalty. A black flag is disqualification.

payload.prompt: If you are chasing a leader and both hit lapped traffic, who gains time?

scene.alt: Two cars catching up to a lapped car.

explanation.correct: Right. The leader slows to pass; the chaser uses the lapped car as a marker and often gets a tow.
explanation.incorrect: The chaser can often benefit from traffic the leader slows for. Traffic is a gamble; sometimes it helps the chaser.

payload.prompt: Can a lapped car defend its position against the car lapping it?

explanation.correct: Right. A lapped car can race until the flag. Once blue is shown, yield immediately.
explanation.incorrect: Before the blue flag, a lapped car can race. Once blue is shown, the lapped car must yield at the next opportunity.

lessons.title: The start and turn one
lessons.objective: Explain how starts are won and lost, including in 2026.

payload.prompt: Tap to launch when the lights go out.

explanation.correct: Perfect timing! A great start is gained on reaction. Balancing perfect launch against a lock-up is the skill.
explanation.incorrect: Late off the line, and you lose positions. Drivers practice the timing endlessly.
explanation.sayThisLine: Split-second timing wins starts.

payload.prompt: How does the MGU-K affect a 2026 start?

options.text: The driver can deploy extra electrical power for a better launch, but must manage the battery carefully.
options.explanation: Right. 2026 starts use the battery. Careful deployment wins or loses a start.

options.text: The MGU-K is not used at the start; it only works during the race.
options.explanation: No. The battery is fully charged at the start and is deployed for launch.

options.text: All drivers get the same electrical power at the start, so starts are purely about reaction.
options.explanation: No. Battery state varies. Teams manage it differently from corner to corner.

options.text: The MGU-K is charged during the race but cannot be used at the start.
options.explanation: Wrong. The battery is fully charged before the start and is available for deployment.

explanation.correct: Right. A full battery at the start is available for launch power. Deploying it well wins the start.
explanation.incorrect: In 2026, the electrical system (MGU-K) is fully charged before the race start. Drivers use it to gain traction off the line.
explanation.sayThisLine: Battery power wins starts in 2026.

payload.prompt: What causes a driver to lose traction off the start line?

options.text: Spinning the tyres (wheelspin) from too much throttle, or locking the brakes under braking.
options.explanation: Right. Wheelspin wastes grip; lock-up wastes braking distance. Both cost positions.

options.text: The track is always slippery at the start.
options.explanation: Not always. Most starts are on clean track. Traction loss is about driver error.

options.text: Too much electrical power always causes wheelspin.
options.explanation: Not if managed well. Too much power without control does cause wheelspin.

options.text: Rain is the only reason for traction loss at the start.
options.explanation: Rain is one reason, but driver inputs (throttle, brakes, electrical power) cause most traction loss.

explanation.correct: Right. Too much throttle spins the tyres; the car does not go forward. Controlling the throttle and the electrical power is the start skill.
explanation.incorrect: Traction loss at the start comes from overdriving the throttle or the electrical system. Smooth, controlled power wins.
explanation.sayThisLine: Smooth throttle wins the start.

payload.prompt: Why is turn one chaos in Formula 1?

options.text: All 20 cars are bunched together, braking from top speed with no tow or dirty air to predict.
options.explanation: Right. Everyone is cold, everyone is packed, the braking is blind, and crashes happen.

options.text: The track is always wet at the start of the race.
options.explanation: Not usually. Wet makes it worse, but even on dry track turn one is chaotic.

options.text: Drivers are always aggressive and love crashing at the start.
options.explanation: Most drivers are careful at turn one. But tight spacing and cold tyres make accidents likely.

options.text: The FIA makes turn one hard on purpose.
options.explanation: No. Turn one is naturally chaotic because 20 cars brake together.

explanation.correct: Right. All 20 cars, cold tyres, cold brakes, no gaps, no traction. Turn one is a lottery and a graveyard.
explanation.incorrect: Turn one is chaos because everyone is braking from speed in a packed field. Tyres are cold, margins are zero, crashes are common.
explanation.sayThisLine: Turn one is lawless; survive it and race from there.

payload.prompt: Does pole position help at the start more on a long straight or a short one?

scene.alt: Track layouts with long and short straights before turn one.

explanation.correct: Right. A short straight to turn one means less time for second place to gain; pole is safer. Long straights give chasers more room.
explanation.incorrect: Pole is most valuable on a short run to turn one. A long straight after the start lets second place gain ground.

payload.prompt: Is a perfect reaction time at the start worth risking a jump-start penalty?

scene.alt: Lights going out at the start.

choices.label: Yes, risk it for the advantage

explanation.correct: Right. A jump-start penalty is 5 seconds. It is not worth the risk. React normally and stay legal.
explanation.incorrect: A jump-start penalty is a race-killer. A normal reaction is worth more than the marginal gain from guessing.
